title: The Lie of the Average: How Class Incremental Learning Evaluation Deceives You?
claim: Standard evaluation samples a few sequences and reports a misleading average that hides worst-case failures; sampling extreme cases reveals the true performance distribution and its bounds.
layout: 3 columns: existing protocol (left, blue dotted box), real distribution with warning message (center), ours (right, red dotted box); each side has a sequence banner on top, a density plot in the middle and a robot speech bubble below
description: The figure has three columns. At the top, two orange arrows read "Incremental Learning Process". Above each arrow's sequence banner sits a pink or gray box: the hardest sequence on the left and the easiest on the right, each shown as a row of vehicle, cone, house and bench icons in a different order. A monitor icon labeled "An Auto-Drive System" sits in the center, and a gray arrow points down from it to a black bell-shaped curve of the real performance distribution. Dotted gray arrows link the two sequence banners to the two tails of that curve. On the left, a blue dotted box shows a narrow blue dashed curve with three blue stars clustered near the mean. A robot's thought bubble says "Your model is safe with an average accuracy of 85%!" and the box is labeled "Existing RS Protocol". On the right, a red dotted box shows a red dashed curve fitted through red diamonds at the tails, and a robot says "Your model may be flawed, with accuracy as low as 70%." The box is labeled "Ours EDGE Protocol". At the bottom center, a double-bordered text box with an alarm icon says the protocol should consider the performance distribution, including upper and lower bounds.
caption: Existing CIL evaluations may be misleading! They merely compute the average accuracy without perceiving the performance distribution, failing to anticipate the impact of potential extreme sequences on the model.
abstract: Class Incremental Learning (CIL) requires models to continuously learn new classes without forgetting previously learned ones, while maintaining stable performance across all possible class sequences. In real-world settings, the order in which classes arrive is diverse and unpredictable, and model performance can vary substantially across different sequences. Yet mainstream evaluation protocols calculate mean and variance from only a small set of randomly sampled sequences. Our theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that this sampling strategy fails to capture the full performance range, resulting in biased mean estimates and a severe underestimation of the true variance in the performance distribution. We therefore contend that a robust CIL evaluation protocol should accurately characterize and estimate the entire performance distribution. To this end, we introduce the concept of extreme sequences and provide theoretical justification for their crucial role in the reliable evaluation of CIL. Moreover, we observe a consistent positive correlation between inter-task similarity and model performance, a relation that can be leveraged to guide the search for extreme sequences. Building on these insights, we propose EDGE (Extreme case-based Distribution & Generalization Evaluation), an evaluation protocol that adaptively identifies and samples extreme class sequences using inter-task similarity, offering a closer approximation of the ground-truth performance distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EDGE effectively captures performance extremes and yields more accurate estimates of distributional boundaries, providing actionable insights for model selection and robustness checking. Our code is available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/EDGE.
